lesson.title: Boss Tweed and the Machine that Ran New York
lesson.summary: Tammany Hall, New York City's Democratic political machine, became the most notorious example of Gilded Age machine politics, reaching its most corrupt extreme under William Boss Tweed before surviving in a more subdued form for decades afterward.
lesson.body:
Tammany Hall began in 1786 as the Tammany Society, a fraternal and patriotic club, but over the course of the nineteenth century it grew into the organizational core of the Democratic Party machine in Manhattan, the clearest and most powerful example of the political machine model at work in any American city.

Tammany's corruption reached its most extreme point under William Marcy Tweed, known as Boss Tweed, who by the late 1860s controlled the organization and, through it, much of New York City and state government. The Tweed Ring skimmed enormous sums of money from city contracts, most infamously during construction of the New York County Courthouse, later nicknamed the Tweed Courthouse, whose final cost ballooned to many times its original estimate through padded bills and kickbacks to Tweed and his associates.

Tweed's downfall came through exposure. Investigative reporting by the New York Times in 1871, combined with the political cartoons of Thomas Nast published in Harper's Weekly, whose images were so effective partly because they could be understood even by voters who could not read, turned public opinion sharply against him. Tweed was indicted and convicted in 1873 and died in a New York City jail in 1878.

Tammany Hall survived Tweed's downfall. Under later bosses such as Richard Croker, it became somewhat less flagrantly corrupt while remaining just as dependent on patronage. One of its ward bosses, George Washington Plunkitt, famously described the distinction between what he called honest graft, personally profiting from advance knowledge of city plans, and dishonest graft, simply stealing outright, in a series of conversations later published by the journalist William Riordon in the 1905 book Plunkitt of Tammany Hall.

Tammany remained a major force in New York politics well into the twentieth century, gradually weakened by Progressive Era reforms and finally broken as a dominant power by reform minded mayors, most notably Fiorello La Guardia in the 1930s. More than any other organization, Tammany Hall illustrates both faces of the political machine: real help delivered to immigrant families who had nowhere else to turn, and a scale of theft from the public that made it a symbol of Gilded Age corruption.
